item.title: DASH Diet UK: What to Eat for High Blood Pressure
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: The DASH diet is an eating plan built to help lower blood pressure: more fruit, veg, wholegrains and low-fat dairy, less salt. Here's a simple UK guide. The DASH diet is an eating plan designed to help lower high blood pressure. It’s built around fruit, vegetables, wholegrains and low-fat dairy, and keeps salt, saturated fat, sugary foods and alcohol low.
item.content:encoded:
The DASH diet is an eating plan designed to help lower high blood pressure. It’s built around fruit, vegetables, wholegrains and low-fat dairy, and keeps salt, saturated fat, sugary foods and alcohol low. You don’t need special foods, just the right balance of everyday ones.

What is the DASH diet?

DASH stands for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) explains that it was designed by researchers at the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute in the 1990s.

The idea is simple: eat less salt (sodium) and more fibre, potassium and calcium. According to the BHF, that combination can help lower blood pressure.

There are no banned foods and no set meals. What matters is getting the balance of food groups right across the day.

Does the DASH diet lower blood pressure?

The BHF says many studies show the DASH diet can help bring blood pressure down to a healthy level. A 2019 review it cites, covering 7 meta-analyses, linked the diet to a 5.2mmHg drop in systolic pressure (the top number) and a 2.6mmHg drop in diastolic pressure (the bottom number).

The same review linked it to a 20 per cent lower risk of cardiovascular disease, including heart attack, stroke and coronary heart disease. Research also suggests it may help with cholesterol, blood sugar and weight.

For context, the BHF says high blood pressure is diagnosed at over 140/90mmHg in a clinic, or over 135/85mmHg for home readings. The NHS notes that high blood pressure doesn’t usually cause any symptoms, so the only way to know is to get it checked.

What can you eat on the DASH diet?

Here are the BHF’s daily servings for someone eating around 2,000 calories a day. If you need more or fewer calories, the number of servings changes.

Food group How much One serving is about
Vegetables 4 to 5 a day 2 handfuls of raw leafy veg, or 1 handful of other veg
Fruit 4 to 5 a day 1 medium fruit, or 3 tbsp unsweetened dried fruit
Wholegrains 7 to 8 a day 1 slice of wholemeal bread, or 1 handful of cooked wholegrain pasta or rice
Lean meat, poultry, fish, eggs Up to 6 a day 30g cooked meat or fish, or 1 egg
Low-fat or fat-free dairy 2 to 3 a day 235ml low-fat milk or yoghurt, or 43g low-fat cheese
Nuts, seeds and beans 4 to 5 a week 43g mixed nuts, 2 tbsp seeds, or 85g cooked beans
Fats and oils 2 to 3 a day 1 tsp vegetable oil or soft margarine
Added sugar and sweets Under 5 a week 1 tbsp sugar or jam
Alcohol Under 1 drink a day, or 14 units a week A single shot of spirit is 1 unit

Vegetables (how much 4 to 5 a day): 2 handfuls of raw leafy veg, or 1 handful of other veg

Fruit (how much 4 to 5 a day): 1 medium fruit, or 3 tbsp unsweetened dried fruit

Wholegrains (how much 7 to 8 a day): 1 slice of wholemeal bread, or 1 handful of cooked wholegrain pasta or rice

Lean meat, poultry, fish, eggs (how much Up to 6 a day): 30g cooked meat or fish, or 1 egg

Low-fat or fat-free dairy (how much 2 to 3 a day): 235ml low-fat milk or yoghurt, or 43g low-fat cheese

Nuts, seeds and beans (how much 4 to 5 a week): 43g mixed nuts, 2 tbsp seeds, or 85g cooked beans

Fats and oils (how much 2 to 3 a day): 1 tsp vegetable oil or soft margarine

Added sugar and sweets (how much Under 5 a week): 1 tbsp sugar or jam

Alcohol (how much Under 1 drink a day, or 14 units a week): a single shot of spirit is 1 unit

That might look like a lot of servings, but the portions are small. A handful of cooked wholegrain rice and a slice of wholemeal toast already make two wholegrain servings.

How much salt is allowed?

The BHF describes two versions of the DASH diet:

  1. Standard: no more than 2,300mg of sodium a day, about 6g or one teaspoon of salt.
  2. Lower sodium: no more than 1,500mg of sodium a day, about 4g or three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt. The BHF says this may lower blood pressure further.

Checking labels makes it easier to stay under the limit. Our guide on how much salt a day shows where it hides and how to spot high-salt foods.

Why does potassium matter?

Blood Pressure UK explains that salt makes your body hold on to water, which upsets the balance of sodium and potassium your kidneys need. Eating more potassium-rich foods helps restore that balance and lets the kidneys help lower your blood pressure.

Good sources it lists include bananas, apricots, potatoes, sweet potatoes, spinach, cabbage, sprouts, fish, yoghurt, nuts and mushrooms. That’s one reason DASH leans so heavily on fruit and veg.

A word of care, though. Blood Pressure UK says that if you have kidney disease or take certain blood pressure medicines, a large increase in potassium could be harmful. It advises avoiding potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes, and checking with your doctor first. The British Dietetic Association adds that if you have kidney disease, speak to your dietitian before changing your diet.

DASH or Mediterranean diet: which is better?

The two have a lot in common. Both are high in fish, vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, nuts and seeds, and low in salt, added sugar, saturated fat and red meat.

The BHF points out a few differences:

  • DASH includes several daily servings of low-fat dairy, because calcium is known to help lower blood pressure
  • the Mediterranean diet recommends more oily fish, a source of omega-3 fats
  • DASH is more structured, with set servings, while the Mediterranean diet is more flexible

The BHF says either can support heart health, so pick the one you can stick with.

Simple ways to start eating the DASH way

You don’t have to change everything at once. A few easy steps:

  • add a portion of fruit or veg to each meal
  • swap white bread, rice and pasta for wholegrain versions
  • switch to semi-skimmed or skimmed milk and plain low-fat yoghurt
  • have beans, lentils or unsalted nuts a few times a week
  • cook from scratch more often, and taste before adding salt
  • keep alcohol within 14 units a week, in line with NHS advice

The NHS also recommends at least 150 minutes of exercise a week alongside a healthy diet. If your blood pressure stays high after lifestyle changes, your GP may suggest medicine. Never stop or change blood pressure tablets yourself; talk to your GP or practice nurse.

Checking meals when there’s no label

Supermarket food has a label, and our guide to reading food labels explains the traffic lights. Meals out and home-cooked dishes don’t. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the salt, sugar and fat in a meal from a photo and suggest a swap that fits a DASH-style plate.

item.title: Is Rice Bad for Diabetes? Portions, Better Choices and Tips
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Rice isn't off limits with diabetes. Portion size matters most, and brown or wholegrain rice is a better pick. See UK portion guides and easy swaps. Is rice bad for diabetes? No, rice can still be part of a healthy diet when you have diabetes. What matters most is how much you eat, because the total amount of carbohydrate has the biggest effect on your blood sugar, and choosing brown or wholegrain rice over white where you can.
item.content:encoded:
Is rice bad for diabetes? No, rice can still be part of a healthy diet when you have diabetes. What matters most is how much you eat, because the total amount of carbohydrate has the biggest effect on your blood sugar, and choosing brown or wholegrain rice over white where you can.

Why does rice raise blood sugar?

Rice is a starchy food, and starchy foods are mostly carbohydrate. Your body breaks carbohydrate down into glucose for energy, which is why your blood sugar goes up after a rice-based meal.

Diabetes UK explains that the total amount of carbohydrate you eat has the biggest effect on your glucose levels after eating. Eating more carbohydrate than usual can push blood sugar too high.

The type of rice matters too. Diabetes UK says cooked white rice is absorbed almost as quickly as glucose from a sugary drink, which gives it a high glycaemic index (GI).

What is the glycaemic index, and where does rice fit?

GI ranks foods and drinks that contain carbohydrate from 0 to 100, based on how quickly they raise blood sugar. Diabetes UK uses these bands:

GI band Score How fast it raises blood sugar
Low 55 or below Slowly
Medium 56 to 69 At a moderate rate
High 70 or more Quickly

Low (score 55 or below): slowly

Medium (score 56 to 69): at a moderate rate

High (score 70 or more): quickly

Diabetes UK lists basmati rice as a medium GI food. It also points out that GI doesn’t account for portion size, and that the amount of carbs you eat has a bigger effect on blood sugar than GI alone.

GI also changes with cooking, processing and what you eat alongside a food. Fat, protein and fibre can all lower the GI of a meal, so rice eaten with vegetables, beans or chicken behaves differently from a plate of rice on its own.

Which rice is best for diabetes?

Diabetes UK suggests choosing brown rice instead of white, and looking out for brown basmati and quick-cook brown rice. Brown rice is a whole grain, so it keeps more of the bran and germ, where most of the nutrients are. When grains are refined, most of that is removed.

According to Diabetes UK, wholegrain foods are usually better for managing blood glucose levels, and choosing high-fibre wholegrains over refined carbs is also better for heart health. The NHS adds that brown and wholegrain rice provide fibre and B vitamins, which help release energy from food.

A quick guide to common choices:

  1. Brown basmati or quick-cook brown rice: a whole grain with more fibre, and the swap Diabetes UK recommends.
  2. White basmati: medium GI, a better pick than standard white rice if you prefer a white grain.
  3. Standard white rice: high GI, so keep portions modest and pair it with vegetables and protein.

Brown rice still contains carbohydrate and still raises blood sugar, so Diabetes UK says it’s worth keeping an eye on portion sizes whichever rice you choose.

How much rice is a portion?

Diabetes UK’s portion guide says a portion of cooked rice is about the amount that would fit in two hands cupped together, around 180g. That’s the same as its guide for boiled pasta and cooked noodles.

Some tips from Diabetes UK for getting portions right:

  • Rice can be tricky to judge at first, so weigh it, then use the same container each time
  • Don’t assume the portion on the packet suits you
  • Try smaller plates and bowls, which make portions look bigger
  • Fill part of your plate with vegetables, which are low in calories and high in fibre
  • Freeze leftover rice dishes in single portions

These portions are a guide for an average healthy adult. A dietitian can tell you the right amount for you.

What can I eat instead of rice?

You don’t have to give rice up, but variety helps. Diabetes UK suggests trying wholewheat couscous, quinoa or bulgur wheat in place of white rice. Adding pulses such as beans and lentils to a meal is another way to bring in fibre.

Fibre is worth the effort. Diabetes UK says it helps keep the digestive system healthy and helps manage blood glucose and cholesterol, and adults should aim for 30g of fibre a day.

If you’re watching carbs, Diabetes UK also says not everyone with diabetes needs to restrict their carb intake. If you take medication that can cause hypos and want to cut down, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian first so they can review it with you.

How should I store and reheat leftover rice?

Leftover rice needs a bit of care. The NHS explains that spores of some food poisoning bugs can survive cooking, and if cooked rice is left at room temperature they can produce toxins that cause vomiting and diarrhoea.

The NHS advice is to:

  • serve rice as soon as it’s cooked, or cool it within 1 hour and keep it in the fridge
  • eat refrigerated rice within 24 hours
  • throw away rice left out at room temperature overnight
  • reheat it only once, until it’s steaming hot all the way through

Checking a rice dish without a label

Packets of rice come with nutrition labels, and our guide on how to read food labels with diabetes explains them. A takeaway curry or a plate of jollof at a family gathering doesn’t. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the carbs in a meal from a photo and suggest a swap, such as a smaller portion of rice with more vegetables. If you’re looking for lighter options between meals, see our best snacks for type 2 diabetes.

item.title: 14 Major Food Allergens UK: What They Are and Where They Hide
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: The 14 major food allergens in the UK, from celery to sulphites, where they hide in everyday food, and how to spot them on labels and menus. The 14 major food allergens in the UK are celery, cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs, mustard, peanuts, sesame, soya, sulphur dioxide and sulphites, and tree nuts.
item.content:encoded:
The 14 major food allergens in the UK are celery, cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs, mustard, peanuts, sesame, soya, sulphur dioxide and sulphites, and tree nuts. UK food law says businesses must tell you when any of them are in the food they sell, whether it’s in a supermarket pack, a bakery counter or a takeaway.

What are the 14 allergens, and where do they hide?

The Food Standards Agency (FSA) describes these 14 as the most potent and common allergens. Some are obvious. Others turn up in places you might not expect.

Allergen What it includes, and what to know
Celery Allergy UK says it’s often hidden in many foods
Cereals containing gluten Wheat, rye, barley and oats
Crustaceans Shellfish such as prawns, crab and lobster
Eggs One of the most common allergies in babies and young children
Fish Part of the wider “seafood” group, along with shellfish
Lupin Less familiar, so check ingredients lists for it
Milk Cow’s milk allergy is one of the most common in UK babies and young children
Molluscs Shellfish such as mussels and oysters
Mustard Allergy UK says it can be hidden, so you may not see, taste or smell it
Peanuts A legume that grows underground, not a tree nut
Sesame Sesame seeds, sesame oil and tahini
Soya Soya flour is common in bread, cakes, ready meals, burgers, sausages and baby foods
Sulphur dioxide and sulphites Preservatives that keep colour, flavour and shelf life, listed above 10 parts per million
Tree nuts Almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, Brazil nuts, cashews, pecans, pistachios and macadamias

Celery: Allergy UK says it’s often hidden in many foods

Cereals containing gluten: Wheat, rye, barley and oats

Crustaceans: Shellfish such as prawns, crab and lobster

Eggs: One of the most common allergies in babies and young children

Fish: Part of the wider “seafood” group, along with shellfish

Lupin: Less familiar, so check ingredients lists for it

Milk: Cow’s milk allergy is one of the most common in UK babies and young children

Molluscs: Shellfish such as mussels and oysters

Mustard: Allergy UK says it can be hidden, so you may not see, taste or smell it

Peanuts: A legume that grows underground, not a tree nut

Sesame: Sesame seeds, sesame oil and tahini

Soya: Soya flour is common in bread, cakes, ready meals, burgers, sausages and baby foods

Sulphur dioxide and sulphites: Preservatives that keep colour, flavour and shelf life, listed above 10 parts per million

Tree nuts: Almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, Brazil nuts, cashews, pecans, pistachios and macadamias

Soya is a good example of how easy it is to miss an allergen. Allergy UK says as many as 60% of manufactured foods contain soya.

Are peanuts and tree nuts the same allergen?

No. Allergy UK points out that peanuts grow underground and belong to the legume family, so they’re listed separately from tree nuts. If you’re not sure which nuts you need to avoid, ask your GP or allergy team.

Which allergies do children grow out of?

Allergy UK says egg and cow’s milk allergies are among the most common in babies and young children. Most children grow out of egg allergy by the time they start school. A small number of people don’t outgrow milk allergy, and Allergy UK says adults who still have it are more likely to have severe reactions.

Tree nut allergies are different. Allergy UK says they tend to last, and people rarely grow out of them, especially after the age of five. If you think your child’s allergy has changed, talk to your GP or allergy team.

How are allergens shown on UK food labels?

On prepacked food, the FSA says any of the 14 allergens must be emphasised in the ingredients list, for example in bold, italics or a different colour. That makes the ingredients list the place to look, not the front of the pack. Our guide on how to read food labels covers the rest of the label.

Since 1 October 2021, food that is prepacked for direct sale (PPDS) must also carry a full ingredients list with the allergens emphasised. The FSA says the label doesn’t replace talking to staff about your allergy.

What does “may contain” mean?

“May contain” or “not suitable for people with a nut allergy” are precautionary labels. They warn that an allergen could be in the food by accident, through cross-contamination during making or packing.

The FSA says there is no specific legal requirement to use these labels, so a food without one isn’t guaranteed to be free of an allergen. If you have a diagnosed allergy, ask your GP or allergy team how to treat “may contain” warnings.

What about loose food, restaurants and takeaways?

You still have the right to know what’s in your food when there’s no label:

  1. Loose food (bakeries, butchers, delis): the business must give you allergen information. It can be written or spoken, but if it’s spoken, staff must tell you where to find it in writing.
  2. Restaurants and cafés: allergen information must be on the menu, or there must be a note telling you how to get it.
  3. Takeaways and delivery: allergen information must be available before you buy and again when the food arrives.

Businesses must give you the information, but they don’t have to make you a different meal. If a business doesn’t provide allergen information, you can report it to the FSA through its “report a food problem” service, which passes it to the local council.

The 14 aren’t the only foods people react to. If your allergen isn’t on the list, the FSA advises checking the label or asking staff.

What are the signs of an allergic reaction?

The NHS lists common symptoms of a food allergy, which can affect several parts of the body at once:

  • itchy skin or a raised rash
  • swelling of the lips, face and eyes
  • sneezing or an itchy, runny or blocked nose
  • coughing, wheezing or a hoarse voice
  • feeling or being sick, tummy pain or diarrhoea
  • feeling dizzy or lightheaded

Symptoms can start straight after eating, or days later. If you think you or your child has a food allergy, see a GP.

When is it an emergency?

Call 999 straight away if lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, breathing becomes fast or difficult, the throat feels tight, skin or lips turn blue, grey or pale, or someone becomes confused, drowsy or faints. These can be signs of anaphylaxis.

If you have an adrenaline auto-injector, the NHS says to use it straight away and then call 999, even if the person seems to be getting better. Don’t drive yourself to A&E.

Checking food when there’s no label

Labels and allergen menus do the heavy lifting, but home cooking, buffets and food from friends don’t come with an ingredients list. An app like Dietary Insight can help you think it through: snap a photo of a meal and it flags ingredients that may contain common allergens on your profile. It can’t see everything in a dish, so always read the full label and ask the person who made the food.

The quick allergen checklist

  1. Learn the 14 allergens, especially the hidden ones like celery, mustard and soya.
  2. Read the ingredients list every time, even on foods you buy often.
  3. Ask staff for allergen information when food is loose, made to order or delivered.
  4. Treat “may contain” warnings the way your GP or allergy team advises.
  5. Carry your adrenaline auto-injector if you’ve been prescribed one.

Read the original article on the Dietary Insight Blog.

item.title: Best Snacks for Type 2 Diabetes: Easy UK Ideas and Swaps
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: The best snacks for type 2 diabetes are fruit, veg, plain yoghurt and unsalted nuts. See calorie and carb counts plus simple swaps for crisps and sweets. The best snacks for type 2 diabetes are simple, everyday foods: fresh fruit, vegetable sticks, plain yoghurt, unsalted nuts and seeds, and wholegrain crackers or oatcakes.
item.content:encoded:
The best snacks for type 2 diabetes are simple, everyday foods: fresh fruit, vegetable sticks, plain yoghurt, unsalted nuts and seeds, and wholegrain crackers or oatcakes. Diabetes UK says snacks can be part of a healthy, balanced diet, as long as you keep an eye on portions and how often you snack.

Do people with type 2 diabetes need to snack?

Not always. An NHS diabetes leaflet from Frimley Health advises that it’s best to avoid extra snacks, especially if you’re trying to lose weight. Eating more wholegrains, fruit, vegetables, beans and pulses at main meals can help you feel fuller for longer.

If you take insulin or certain medications that can cause hypos, you may need a snack between meals. Diabetes UK says this should contain some starchy carbohydrate. If you find you need frequent snacks to avoid low blood sugar, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian.

What makes a good diabetes snack?

The Frimley Health leaflet suggests snacks with about 10 to 15g of carbohydrate and a low to medium glycaemic index (GI). Diabetes UK adds a few pointers:

  • choose snacks that are lower in saturated fat, sugar and salt
  • keep healthier snacks at home and take some out with you
  • check whether you’re really thirsty, not hungry; water or unsweetened tea or coffee may be all you need
  • skip foods labelled “diabetic”, which have no proven special benefit

Snack amounts vary by brand and pack size, so check the label on anything pre-packed. Our guide on how to read food labels with diabetes explains the traffic lights.

Which snacks are under 100 calories?

These figures come from Diabetes UK. They’re handy if you’re watching your weight as well as your blood sugar.

Snack Calories
1 kiwi fruit 25
80g blueberries 32
1 small apple (about 85g) 37
2 satsumas 44
1 light cheese triangle and 4 cherry tomatoes 43
10 almonds 61
1 crispbread, 25g cottage cheese and 4 cherry tomatoes 75
50g roasted chickpeas 79
100g cherries with 50g natural yoghurt 87.5
50g baked plantain chips 100

1 kiwi fruit: 25 calories

80g blueberries: 32 calories

1 small apple (about 85g): 37 calories

2 satsumas: 44 calories

1 light cheese triangle and 4 cherry tomatoes: 43 calories

10 almonds: 61 calories

1 crispbread, 25g cottage cheese and 4 cherry tomatoes: 75 calories

50g roasted chickpeas: 79 calories

100g cherries with 50g natural yoghurt: 87.5 calories

50g baked plantain chips: 100 calories

A little more filling, at under 150 calories: 125g natural yoghurt with 80g raspberries (119), or a 25g slice of Edam with a small apple (122).

Which snacks are lowest in carbs?

Diabetes UK lists these snacks with under 10g of carbohydrate:

  1. 1 chopped boiled egg: 0g carbs, 79 calories
  2. Half an avocado (70g): 1g carbs, 133 calories
  3. 115g pot of sugar-free jelly: 1.2g carbs, 8 calories
  4. 30g almonds: 2g carbs, 184 calories
  5. 30g houmous with 80g sliced peppers: 5g carbs, 104 calories
  6. 1 kiwi fruit: 5g carbs, 25 calories
  7. Homemade vegetable crisps: 8.4g carbs, 48 calories

Low carb doesn’t always mean low calorie. Nuts give you fibre and healthy fats, but Diabetes UK suggests watching portions if you’re managing your weight.

What can I swap for crisps, chocolate and sweets?

You don’t have to give up the snacks you love. Diabetes UK suggests these swaps:

Instead of Try
Crisps Plain popcorn, with a pinch of cinnamon if you like
Bombay mix A small handful of unsalted pumpkin or sunflower seeds
White pitta and dips Wholemeal pitta, or carrot and celery sticks with homemade hummus
Milk chocolate Two or three squares of dark chocolate
Ice cream Frozen banana, or frozen unsweetened yoghurt with berries
Chocolate biscuits Plain biscuits such as rich tea or plain digestives
Sweets Frozen grapes or frozen blueberries
Salted nuts Unsalted nuts
Sugary fizzy drinks Water flavoured with mint or fresh fruit

Instead of crisps, try plain popcorn, with a pinch of cinnamon if you like

Instead of bombay mix, try a small handful of unsalted pumpkin or sunflower seeds

Instead of white pitta and dips, try wholemeal pitta, or carrot and celery sticks with homemade hummus

Instead of milk chocolate, try two or three squares of dark chocolate

Instead of ice cream, try frozen banana, or frozen unsweetened yoghurt with berries

Instead of chocolate biscuits, try plain biscuits such as rich tea or plain digestives

Instead of sweets, try frozen grapes or frozen blueberries

Instead of salted nuts, try unsalted nuts

Instead of sugary fizzy drinks, try water flavoured with mint or fresh fruit

If you enjoy nut butter, check the label. Diabetes UK notes that some contain added sugar, salt or palm oil.

What about plantain chips, patties and other world snacks?

Diabetes UK looked at popular snacks from South Asian, African and Caribbean shops. Some pack a lot of carbs into one bag. For example, a 42.5g bag of sweet plantain chips has 27.7g of carbs and 204 calories, and a 140g jerk chicken patty has 39.3g of carbs and 345.5 calories.

Diabetes UK says the plantain chips and patty are high in saturated fat and carbs, so keep portions small. As an occasional treat, it says snacks like these can be part of a healthy diet. It suggests measuring out a portion before you reseal the packet and keeping the rest out of sight. For something you can have more often, try spicy roasted chickpeas, baked plantain chips or homemade veg crisps.

How do I stop snacking when I’m not hungry?

Boredom, emotions, nerves and anxiety can all send us to the snack cupboard. Diabetes UK suggests pausing to ask why you’re reaching for food, then trying a distraction such as calling a friend, reading or going for a walk. And if you do snack, don’t beat yourself up about it.

Late-night snacking is worth watching too. You use less energy while you sleep, so Diabetes UK says late-night snacks can lead to weight gain and affect how you manage your diabetes.

Checking snacks without a label

Packets make portions easy to compare, but a plate of leftovers or a bakery treat rarely comes with numbers. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the carbs and calories in a snack from a photo and suggest a swap, so you can see how it fits into your day. For more ideas earlier in the day, see our diabetes-friendly breakfast ideas.

item.title: 12 Diabetes-Friendly Breakfast Ideas (UK Guide)
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Simple breakfasts for type 2 diabetes built on fibre, protein and wholegrains, plus the cereal and juice traps to avoid. Quick UK ideas inside. A good breakfast for type 2 diabetes combines slow-release carbs, fibre and some protein . That mix tends to raise blood sugar more gently and keeps you full until lunch.
item.content:encoded:
A good breakfast for type 2 diabetes combines slow-release carbs, fibre and some protein. That mix tends to raise blood sugar more gently and keeps you full until lunch. There’s no special “diabetes diet”, so these are ordinary foods you can buy in any UK supermarket.

What makes a breakfast diabetes-friendly

  • Low-GI starchy foods: oats, wholegrain or multigrain bread, and wholegrain cereal instead of white bread or sugary cereal.
  • Fibre: adults should aim for 30g a day, and breakfast is an easy place to start.
  • Protein: eggs, plain yoghurt, milk, nuts or seeds help you stay full.
  • Little or no free sugar: watch the honey, syrup, jam, juice and flavoured yoghurts.

12 breakfast ideas

Quick (under 5 minutes)

  1. Porridge with berries. Make it with milk or water and add a handful of berries and a pinch of cinnamon instead of sugar.
  2. Plain Greek yoghurt with fruit and seeds. Choose unsweetened yoghurt and add berries, sliced apple or a spoon of seeds.
  3. Wholegrain toast with peanut butter. Use a thin spread of a no-added-sugar peanut butter.
  4. Wholegrain cereal with milk. Pick a cereal with green or amber for sugar, and check the per 100g figure.
  5. Melon or grapefruit with unsweetened yoghurt. A light option Diabetes UK suggests.
  6. Overnight oats. Oats soaked in milk overnight, topped with berries in the morning.

When you have more time

  1. Scrambled or poached eggs on wholegrain toast.
  2. Vegetable omelette. Peppers, spinach, mushrooms and onions.
  3. Beans on wholegrain toast. Choose reduced-sugar and reduced-salt baked beans.
  4. Smoked salmon with egg. Keep it as a treat, because smoked fish is salty.
  5. Shakshuka. Eggs baked in a spiced tomato and pepper sauce.
  6. Wholegrain pancakes. Top with berries and yoghurt instead of syrup.

Breakfast traps to watch

Instead of Try
Sugary or chocolate cereal Porridge or a plain wholegrain cereal
Fruit juice or a smoothie A piece of whole fruit and a glass of water
White toast with jam Wholegrain toast with eggs or peanut butter
Flavoured fruit yoghurt Plain yoghurt with fresh berries
Pastries and croissants Overnight oats or a vegetable omelette

Instead of sugary or chocolate cereal, try porridge or a plain wholegrain cereal

Instead of fruit juice or a smoothie, try a piece of whole fruit and a glass of water

Instead of white toast with jam, try wholegrain toast with eggs or peanut butter

Instead of flavoured fruit yoghurt, try plain yoghurt with fresh berries

Instead of pastries and croissants, try overnight oats or a vegetable omelette

Juice and smoothies count as free sugars, and they have less fibre than whole fruit. A glass of juice can raise blood sugar quickly, even with “no added sugar” on the label.

Portions still matter

A big bowl of a healthy cereal is still a lot of carbohydrate. Use a measured portion for a week to learn what one looks like. If you use insulin or medicines that can cause low blood sugar, talk to your diabetes team before changing your breakfast routine.

Check your breakfast in seconds

Not sure about a café breakfast or a new cereal? Snap a photo with Dietary Insight to see the sugar, fibre and protein, plus a healthier swap if there’s a better option.

Read the original article on the Dietary Insight Blog.

item.title: How Much Salt a Day? A UK Guide for High Blood Pressure
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Adults should have no more than 6g of salt a day. Here's where it hides, how to read salt on labels and easy swaps to cut back. Adults in the UK should have no more than 6g of salt a day , about one level teaspoon. Eating too much salt can raise blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes.
item.content:encoded:
Adults in the UK should have no more than 6g of salt a day, about one level teaspoon. Eating too much salt can raise blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Most of it isn’t from the salt shaker.

Where your salt really comes from

The NHS says about three quarters of the salt we eat is already in food when we buy it. The biggest sources are everyday foods:

  • bread and breakfast cereals
  • ham, bacon, sausages and other processed meat
  • ready meals, takeaways and restaurant food
  • sauces such as soy sauce, gravy granules, ketchup and brown sauce
  • cheese, olives, pickles and smoked or cured fish

None of these tastes especially salty, which is why salt is easy to overdo.

Daily salt limits by age

Age Maximum salt a day
Adults and children 11+ 6g
7 to 10 years 5g
4 to 6 years 3g
1 to 3 years 2g
Under 1 year Less than 1g

Adults and children 11+: 6g

7 to 10 years: 5g

4 to 6 years: 3g

1 to 3 years: 2g

Under 1 year: Less than 1g

Salt or sodium? Do the conversion

Some labels list sodium instead of salt. Multiply sodium by 2.5 to get the salt figure. So 0.6g of sodium is 1.5g of salt, which is already a quarter of an adult’s daily limit.

Reading salt on a food label

Per 100g of food:

  • Low (green): 0.3g of salt or less
  • High (red): more than 1.5g of salt

Compare similar products per 100g. Two loaves or two jars of pasta sauce can differ a lot.

8 easy swaps to cut back

  1. Cook from scratch more often, so you control the salt.
  2. Flavour food with herbs, spices, garlic, chilli, lemon or black pepper.
  3. Taste before you add salt at the table, or leave the shaker in the cupboard.
  4. Choose reduced-salt stock cubes and gravy, and use less.
  5. Swap processed meat sandwiches for chicken, egg or bean fillings.
  6. Rinse tinned beans and vegetables canned in brine.
  7. Ask for sauces on the side when you eat out.
  8. Snack on unsalted nuts, fruit or veg sticks instead of crisps.

Your taste buds adjust within a few weeks, and food that once tasted bland starts to taste normal.

A word on salty medicines

Some dissolvable tablets, such as certain painkillers and vitamins, contain a surprising amount of salt. Don’t stop any medicine on your own. Ask your GP or pharmacist whether there’s a lower-salt version.

Checking meals without a label

Takeaways and restaurant food are some of the saltiest meals, and they rarely show a figure. An app like Dietary Insight can estimate the salt in a meal from a photo, so you can see when one dish uses up most of your day’s allowance.

item.title: How to Read UK Food Labels When You Have Diabetes
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: A simple guide to UK traffic-light labels, hidden sugar names and per-100g figures, so you can choose better food in the supermarket in seconds. Most UK food packs carry a traffic-light label on the front. Learn three numbers and you can judge sugar, fat and salt in a few seconds, without a calculator.
item.content:encoded:
Most UK food packs carry a traffic-light label on the front. Learn three numbers and you can judge sugar, fat and salt in a few seconds, without a calculator.

The traffic-light label in 10 seconds

Green means low, amber means medium and red means high. A pack that is mostly green and amber is a good everyday choice. Any red means that food is best eaten less often or in smaller amounts.

These are the NHS thresholds per 100g of food:

Per 100g Low (green) High (red)
Total fat 3g or less More than 17.5g
Saturated fat 1.5g or less More than 5g
Sugars 5g or less More than 22.5g
Salt 0.3g or less More than 1.5g

Total fat (low (green) 3g or less): more than 17.5g

Saturated fat (low (green) 1.5g or less): more than 5g

Sugars (low (green) 5g or less): more than 22.5g

Salt (low (green) 0.3g or less): more than 1.5g

Anything between the two columns is amber. Drinks use different thresholds, so treat these figures as a guide for food.

Always compare per 100g, not per portion

Manufacturers choose their own portion sizes, and they are often smaller than what people really eat. When you compare two cereals or two yoghurts, use the per 100g column. It’s the only fair comparison.

Quick tip: if you’d eat twice the “portion” on the pack, double every number on the front label.

Spot hidden sugar in the ingredients

Ingredients are listed by weight, with the biggest first. Sugar often hides under other names, and a product can use several of them so none appears near the top. Look out for:

  • glucose, fructose, sucrose, dextrose, maltose
  • corn syrup and high-fructose corn syrup
  • honey, molasses, treacle, maple syrup and agave syrup
  • fruit juice concentrate and fruit purées
  • cane sugar and brown sugar

UK guidance says adults should have no more than 30g of free sugars a day, about 7 sugar cubes. Free sugars include sugar added to food and the sugar in honey, syrups and fruit juice. They don’t include the sugar naturally found in whole fruit, vegetables and milk.

Why “total sugars” can mislead

The label shows total sugars, which mixes natural and added sugar. A plain yoghurt shows some sugar from milk, which is fine. A fruit yoghurt might show double that because of added sugar. Check the ingredients list to tell them apart.

Skip foods labelled “diabetic”

Diabetes UK advises against foods sold as “diabetic”. They have no proven benefit, they often cost more, and some are still high in fat and calories. A normal, balanced choice is better.

When there is no label

Restaurant meals, takeaways and home cooking don’t come with a traffic light. That’s where most of us guess. Fill half the plate with vegetables or salad, keep starchy carbs to about a quarter, and choose grilled over fried where you can.

You can also photograph the plate with an app such as Dietary Insight. It estimates the sugar, salt and fat in the meal and flags anything that clashes with your health profile.

The 3-second checklist

  1. Look for red on the front. More red means “sometimes”, not “every day”.
  2. Compare similar products using the per 100g figures.
  3. Scan the first three ingredients for sugar under another name.

item.title: What Is Prediabetes and Can It Be Reversed? A UK Guide
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Prediabetes means blood sugar is above normal but below type 2 diabetes. Learn the HbA1c numbers, who is at risk and the changes that can help. Prediabetes means your blood sugar is higher than normal but not high enough to be type 2 diabetes. It’s sometimes called borderline diabetes. And can it be reversed?
item.content:encoded:
Prediabetes means your blood sugar is higher than normal but not high enough to be type 2 diabetes. It’s sometimes called borderline diabetes. And can it be reversed? Diabetes UK says yes, it’s possible: with health changes, many people bring their blood sugar back into the normal range, though there’s no guarantee.

What is prediabetes, exactly?

Prediabetes is a state where the sugar in your blood is above normal but below the threshold for type 2 diabetes. It’s diagnosed with a blood test, and results are often given as an HbA1c number.

Diabetes UK estimates it affects around one in 12 people. Without changes, it doesn’t go away on its own, and it puts you at higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes.

What do the HbA1c numbers mean?

Your result will be given in mmol/mol. Here’s how Diabetes UK groups the numbers:

HbA1c result What it means
Below 42 mmol/mol Normal range
42 to 47 mmol/mol Prediabetes
48 mmol/mol or above Type 2 diabetes range

Below 42 mmol/mol: Normal range

42 to 47 mmol/mol: Prediabetes

48 mmol/mol or above: Type 2 diabetes range

If your result is in the prediabetes range, your GP should talk to you about next steps and how often to have it checked again.

Who is more likely to get prediabetes?

Prediabetes is more common in people living with overweight or obesity, but it can affect people of a healthy weight too. Diabetes UK is clear that weight alone doesn’t cause it. It comes from a mix of factors that differ from person to person.

Some risk factors you can’t change:

  • Age.
  • Family history and genetics.
  • Ethnicity: people of Black African, African Caribbean and South Asian backgrounds have a higher risk of type 2 diabetes than people of White European backgrounds, and may develop it at a younger age or a lower body weight.
  • Gestational diabetes: women who had diabetes in pregnancy are among those at highest risk.

Others you can work on, such as how active you are, carrying weight around your middle, diet, sleep and smoking.

Can prediabetes be reversed?

Diabetes UK says it is possible. In practice, “reversing” prediabetes means your HbA1c goes back below 42 mmol/mol.

It’s worth being realistic. Diabetes UK says there’s no guarantee it will work for everyone, and bringing it down within three months is unlikely. Even if your number doesn’t drop all the way, any reduction can help keep it out of the type 2 range and can help with cholesterol and blood pressure too.

What changes can help?

These are the main areas Diabetes UK suggests. Speak to your GP before you make big changes to your diet, weight or activity, especially if you take any medication.

  1. Lose some weight, if you need to. If you’re living with overweight or obesity, weight loss is likely to have the biggest impact. Diabetes UK says losing around 1% to 9% of your body weight can lower your risk. Not everyone with prediabetes needs to lose weight.
  2. Eat more whole foods. Fill up on fruit, vegetables, fibre and wholegrains, such as brown rice and multigrain bread instead of white.
  3. Cut back on a few things. Eat less salt, red meat and processed meat, and avoid sugary drinks.
  4. Move more and sit less. Start by breaking up long spells of sitting. If you’re at a desk or in front of the TV, get up and move every 30 to 45 minutes. Activity that leaves you slightly out of breath, like a brisk walk, is especially helpful.
  5. Sleep well and stop smoking. Poor sleep and smoking can both raise your risk of high blood sugar. Your GP can point you to NHS support to quit.

Pick one change and build from there. Diabetes UK gives the example of swapping sugary fizzy drinks for diet versions for a month. If breakfast is a weak spot, our diabetes-friendly breakfast ideas are a good place to start.

What is the NHS Healthier You programme?

If you have prediabetes, your GP should refer you to a free type 2 diabetes prevention course or offer prevention advice, depending on where you live. In England, this is the NHS Healthier You programme.

According to NHS England:

  • it lasts nine months
  • you can do it in face-to-face group sessions or through a digital service with online content, health coaches and peer support
  • it covers healthier eating, keeping to a healthy weight and staying active
  • nearly one million people in England have started it since 2016

NHS England reports that participants lost 3.3kg on average, and that a review found completing the programme was linked to a 37% lower chance of developing type 2 diabetes.

How do I find out if I’m at risk?

Because prediabetes usually has no symptoms, a blood test is the only way to know. Diabetes UK has a free online Know Your Risk tool that gives you a personal risk score. If your score is high, or you have any of the risk factors above, ask your GP about an HbA1c test.

If you’ve already been told you have prediabetes, keep going to your follow-up checks so you can see how your changes are working.

Making everyday meals easier to judge

Small food changes add up, but it can be hard to know what’s in a meal when there’s no label to check. If you’re buying packaged food, our guide on how to read food labels with diabetes explains the traffic lights. For home-cooked meals and takeaways, the Dietary Insight app can estimate the carbs and sugar in a dish from a photo and suggest a swap, which can help you spot patterns over time.

Prediabetes is a warning sign, not a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. For advice that fits your health, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian.
